## INTRODUCTION

The cultivation of cucumber is one of the horticultural crops identified by CENTA to study its productive problems and transfer new technologies generated and validated with the aim that producers obtain high-quality and profitable productions.

To achieve this objective, the Executive Directorate of CENTA, through the Vegetable Program of the Technology Research Management, makes this available so that it serves as a tool for dissemination and consultation for horticulturists, related professionals, students and the general public, on the advances of research and the use of agronomic and cultural practices that require the cultivation.

To facilitate the consultation of this guide, its content is presented in chapters, with greater emphasis on those aspects related to the agronomic management of the varieties, protection of the crop and marketing.

## IMPORTANCE:

Cucumber belongs to the Cucurbitaceae family and its scientific name is Cucumis sativus. According to data from the DGEA (2000), it reports that for the 1998-1999 period, 437,125 kg were imported for a value of 73,398.17 dollars. This indicates that there is an unsatisfied internal demand. This crop represents an alternative for Salvadoran farmers to diversify and satisfy the demand of the domestic market and for export purposes. To achieve this purpose, it is necessary to carry out staggered plantings to maintain a constant presence in the market, take advantage of the price seasonality and increase the planting areas with high-yielding hybrid materials. In addition, cucumber is one of the vegetables that our population consumes more and more, either fresh or pickled.

## ORIGIN:

It is native to the tropical regions of Southern Asia, cultivated for 3,000 years in the Northwest of India, later it was transferred to other parts of the world, especially in America.

## NUTRITIONAL VALUE:

Regarding its nutritional content, it is one of the vegetables that contains vitamins A, B, and C, as well as minerals, which are essential in human nutrition.

## BOTANICAL ASPECTS:

## SEED:

It is oval-shaped, white-yellow in color, and is protected by a hard covering. Its size is 8 to 10 mm in length with a thickness of 3 to 5 mm.

## GERMINATION:

The germination period varies from 3 to 4 days under favorable conditions.

## ROOT:

## STEM:

It is a vine with a main stem that gives rise to several lateral branches, mainly at the base, between the first 20 and 30 cm, dividing into primary and secondary lateral branches. These stems can reach up to 3.5 m in length under normal conditions. The tendrils help the plant to grip the surfaces.

Photo 4. Cucumber stem

<!-- image -->

The root system consists of a main root that reaches 1.0 to 1.2 m and branches in all directions, mainly between the first 25 to 30 cm of soil length,

<!-- image -->

Photo 3, Cucumber cultivation root

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## LEAVES:

<!-- image -->

They are simple, heart-shaped, petiolate, palminervate, alternate, but opposite the tendrils, they are rough and have 3 to 5 angular and triangular lobes, with a thin cuticle that minimizes excessive transpiration.

Photo 5. Cucumber leaves

<!-- image -->

The plant has flowers of both sexes on the same plant, so it is considered monoic, with cross-pollination; some varieties have hermaphrodite flowers. At the beginning, only male flowers appear in the lower part of the plant, in the center, in equal proportion, the male and female flowers and in the upper part the female flowers predominate. The male and female flowers are located in the axils of the secondary branches.

The male flowers have a heart-shaped calyx with 5 acuminated teeth in the shape of a saw, the corolla attached to the calyx, in the shape of a bell, veined, wrinkled and with 5 divisions; the central disc is trigonal, truncated, covered by the stamens, which are in number of 3.

The female flowers have the calyx and corolla the same as the male flowers, 3 sterile filaments, a style and 3 bífid stigmas. Generally, short days, low temperatures and sufficient water, induce the formation of a greater number of female flowers; but if the days are long, high temperatures and drought, these conditions favor the formation of male flowers.

Pollination is carried out in the field, mainly through bees. The productivity of the crop will largely depend on the number of female flowers it has, as these will become fruits.

## FRUIT:

It is considered a false berry (peponid), elongated and cylindrical, measuring between 15 and 35 cm in length, depending on the crop. It is a fleshy fruit, white inside and green or light green outside, rough and warty; in its young stage, the fruits have white or black false spines on the surface, which are waxy; in its juvenile stage, which falls off, is the optimal harvest time and in its mature stage, it has a yellow color.

## PHENOLOGY

The cucumber cycle is short and varies from place to place depending on the edaphoclimatic conditions of the crop and the agronomic management it receives during its development; however, under the climatic conditions of El Salvador, the cucumber has the following phenological cycle:

| PHENOLOGICAL STAGE          | DAYS AFTER SOWING.   |
|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| Emergence                 | 4-5                        |
| Start of guide emergence | 15-24                      |
| Start of flowering        | 27-34                      |
| Start of harvest          | 43-50                      |
| End of harvest             | 75-90                      |

## CLIMATIC AND AGE REQUIREMENTS

## ALTITUDE:

The crop adapts very well to altitudes of 0 to 1,200 m above sea level, depending on the cultivar.

## TEMPERATURE:

This crop develops very well with temperatures of 18 to 25°C, above 40°C, the plant growth stops, when below 14°C, the growth ceases and the plants die when the temperature drops below 1°C.

## RELATIVE HUMIDITY:

This crop develops well when the relative humidity is low, when it is high, the plants become susceptible to fungal disease attacks. Table 2 allows us to know the optimal range of this factor.

## PRECIPITATION:

It needs relatively low precipitation, to reduce the incidence of diseases, especially during harvest.

## PHOTOPERIOD:

This plant is affected by the amount of light received. When the days are short, it induces the formation of more female flowers, and long days favor the formation of male flowers, so it is a crop influenced by the photoperiod.

## WIND:

The yield of this crop is affected by the intensity of the wind, with a speed of more than 30 km/h for a period of 4 to 6 hours, it produces a significant reduction in production.

## SOIL:

Cucumber can be grown in a wide range of soils, from sandy to loamy, the ideal ones for its good development are loamy soils with abundant organic matter (more than 3.5%). These soils should contain an effective depth greater than 60 cm, which facilitates the retention of water and the growth of the root system, so that the plant achieves good development and excellent yield. It should be avoided to plant in soils that are too clayey, which causes waterlogging, which favors the development of fungal diseases, especially powdery mildew. It adapts very well to a pH range of 5.5 to 6.8, tolerating up to 7.5. It should be avoided to plant in acidic soils with a pH of less than 5.5.

## VARIETIES

In El Salvador, there are production areas that still plant traditional open-pollinated varieties; however, in recent years, the planting of hybrid materials has increased (Table No. 3).

Hybrids can have the following flowering habits: monoic, in which the plants have both male and female flowers, or ginoic, in which the plants have 100% female flowers. In this case, it is necessary to use the seed of another variety as a pollinator at 10% to 15%. This characteristic makes this type of hybrid have a greater potential for production and precociousness compared to monoic hybrids; however, they are less vigorous. Their advantages and disadvantages are summarized as follows:

<!-- image -->

## Varieties of open pollination.

Lower yield; greater susceptibility to diseases; preferred by the fruit borer (Diaphania nitidalis).

## Hybrids.

Higher yields; greater tolerance to pests and diseases, such as the fruit borer and powdery mildew; healthy and vigorous plants; better quality of the product, with fruits of greater weight, good color, uniform shape and resistant to transport

## CULTURAL PRACTICES

For cucumber planting, it is necessary to consider the following conditions:

- Do not repeat the cucumber crop in the same soil for more than one season.
- Exhibits good development in places where bulbs and roots have been previously planted.
- Should not be planted after another cucurbit crop (melon, pumpkin, etc.).
- The chosen soil must meet the requirements of the crop in terms of pH and water availability for irrigation.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## SOIL SAMPLING:

Since cucumbers are susceptible to nematode and soil fungal attacks, to prevent any problems before planting, it is recommended to take soil samples for their respective phytopathological, nematological, and chemical analysis.

## SOIL PREPARATION

It should begin as early as possible before planting, in order to promote pest control, allow for proper incorporation and decomposition of vegetable residues in the soil. The soil should be well leveled, firm, and have a uniform texture. Soil preparation operations will vary depending on the terrain, and will be subject to factors that occurred in the preparation of soil in previous crops, the presence of a plow, the type of weeds, the moisture content, and the farmer's economic capacity to properly manage the crop. The soil preparation sequence is as follows:

## SUBSOILING:

If there are compaction problems such as a plow, it is recommended to perform a subsoiling at a depth of 60 cm:

## PLOWING:

Plowing is necessary to perform a plowing at a depth of 30 to 40 cm

## RUSTLING:

It is recommended to perform at least two rustling passes, at a depth of 30 cm, to incorporate the stems and break up clods

## TILLING:

This is done with a single pass of the rotary cultivator, so that the soil is well loosened (free of clods).

## SOWING BED:

This is constructed with a single pass of the rotary cultivator, leaving a sowing bed of 1.2 m wide and 25 to 30 cm high.

It is recommended to raise the bed or sowing bed at least 20 to 25 cm, to provide adequate drainage for the crop, especially during the rainy season.

## PLANTING SEASONS:

It is possible to cultivate throughout the year, both in the dry and rainy seasons, as long as there is water availability for irrigation. To obtain better prices in the market, it should be sown in the months of March, August, September and October, with the last one presenting fewer problems of pests and diseases; May plantings present fewer problems of virus, but can increase diseases, irrigation.

Therefore, it is recommended to establish a preventive program of application of fungicides, to prevent the appearance of diseases caused by fungi.

## PLANTING

This consists of manually placing the seeds in the soil with a hoe or stake, in rows according to the recommended spacing for the crop. In this system, the incorporation of insecticides and fertilizers is done in a previous task, to avoid that they come into direct contact with the seeds.

## PLANTING SPACING:

In cucumber cultivation, the spacing varies according to the planting system used, the soil texture, the climate, local cultural practices and the time of year, irrigation.

However, the spacing between rows can vary between 0.80 m and 1.50 m; between plants 0.15 m. The population density will depend on the spacing used. Two seeds are placed per plant, requiring between 2 and 3 pounds of seed per plant, depending on the planting system used.

## PLANTING SYSTEMS

This is a plant that can freely extend its foliage over the ground or climb with the help of its tendrils. It is commonly cultivated on the ground; to avoid the additional cost of building a structure to support it; however, the cost of trellising is compensated by the amount and quality of the product, obtaining greater income.

## ON THE GROUND:

Cucumber cultivation on the ground can take several modalities: the availability of equipment for tillage, the irrigation system and the level of technological development of the farmer. The most appropriate is to use a raised bed, firm and uniform, on which the planting line is placed, so that the foliage of the plants never comes into direct contact with the soil, it is necessary to place a material that serves as mulch according to irrigation.

## TRELLISING (TRELLIS):

This system is used to guide the plants, taking into account their climbing habit and indeterminate growth. It is recommended to offer the following advantages: better use of solar energy, good arrangement of the leaves, greater ventilation inside the planting, more homogeneous fruit color and shape, greater plant populations per area and easier harvesting.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## TYPES OF TRELLISES:

## FLAT INCLINED TRELLIS:

Bamboo or wooden stakes of 2.5 m in length are used; the vertical stake is buried 0.5 m, the distance between the stakes in the row is 4.0 m, the first row of galvanized wire #18 or nylon tape is placed at a height of 0.3 m, the second and third rows of tape are placed 0.5 m apart from each other. The construction of the trellises should begin before the plants start to form guides.

## TRELLIS TYPE "A"=

Two stakes are used, joined at the top and separated by 1.0 to 1.3 m on the ground. The planting is done in rows on both sides of the trellis.

Photo 13. Trellis Type A

<!-- image -->

## VERTICAL TRELLIS:

Stakes are placed every 4.0 m on the rows of the crop, and 3 or 4 rows of nylon tape horizontally, to form a net, by placing thread between the rows of nylon tape in a zig-zag, where the plants are located to climb, and not have contact with the ground. The lifespan of the stakes depends on the type of wood used, but it can serve for 3-4 plantings on average. stake,

## FOLIAR FERTILIZATION:

It has been observed that foliar applications of fertilizers contribute significantly to the prolongation of the harvest and the quality of the products. In this regard, the following application program is suggested: follow

- 7 days after planting or transplanting, apply Bayfolan Forte 75 at a concentration of 4 gallons, plus 20 cc of zinc supplement.
- 21 days after planting or transplanting, apply Metalosato multimineral 100 at a concentration of 4 gallons, plus 25 cc of calcium supplement.
- 14 days after planting or transplanting, apply Foliar Forte 50 per 4 gallons pump, plus 15 cc of boron supplement.
- 29 days after planting or transplanting, apply Bayfolan forte 75 at a concentration of 4 gallons, plus 15 cc of boron supplement
- 45 days after planting or transplanting, apply triple 20, plus 25 CC of magnesium supplement.
- 37 days after planting or transplanting, apply Foliar Forte 50 per 4 gallons pump, plus 15 cc of boron supplement

## APPLICATION OF CALCIUM

To apply calcium or a calcium application on the soil, the following should be taken into account:

- Calcium applications should be made at least 2 months before planting cucumbers, according to the dosage indicated in the result of a soil analysis.
- It is necessary to have the result of a soil analysis beforehand.
- Calcium should be applied to the surface and incorporated into the soil.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

- The maximum amount that is recommended for a calcium application is 1280 1300 kg/ha or 900 kg/mz if a larger amount is applied, it can cause an imbalance with magnesium and potassium.
- If magnesium levels are low, as a result of soil analysis, it is recommended to use dolomite lime.
- The change will be gradual, for example: it should first go from 4 to 5 and then to 6. It is not correct to try to bring the pH from 4 to 6 with a single application. pH

## BENEFITS OF CALCIUM APPLICATION:

- Improves the physical condition of the soil
- Improves nitrogen fixation.
- The increase in pH reduces the excess of soluble manganese, aluminum and iron in the soil.
- Improves the content of calcium and magnesium.
- Increases the availability of nitrogen and increases the decomposition of organic matter.
- Calcium makes phosphorus more available in acidic soils.
- Improves the availability of micronutrients.
- Improves nitrification.
- Makes potassium more efficient in plant nutrition.
- Increases the availability of molybdenum in acidic soils.

## NUTRITIONAL DISORDERS OF PEPPER CULTIVATION

NITROGEN: A deficiency of this mineral delays growth, the foliage takes on a lighter green color, the discoloration is more pronounced in the older leaves; the main veins of the leaves remain green contrasting with the rest of the blade. The fruits take on a pale yellow color and a pointed shape; when the deficiency is severe, the entire plant turns yellow, the cotyledons and young leaves.

PHOSPHORUS: In general, the cucumber plant does not show very clear symptoms in the face of a phosphorus deficiency; to detect the problem, refer to the foliar analysis. When the deficiency is severe, the growth stops, leaving the young leaves small and rigid, while the older ones show bluish spots that turn brown

POTASSIUM: Although its deficiency is not very frequent in the soils of El Salvador, deficiencies can occur in certain areas. The most visible symptoms that are observed are the cessation of growth and the shortening of the internodes; at the same time, the leaves and edges turn green and yellow. As the deficiency of this element progresses, the chlorosis between the veins becomes more pronounced and approaches the center of the leaf; on the other hand, it progresses from the base upwards; the older leaves are the most affected; the fruits, in turn, lose firmness, influencing their weight and conservation.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

MAGNESIUM: The most common nutritional imbalance problem in cucumber cultivation is the lack of magnesium. The lack of this element can be due to the blockage at high potassium levels. The lack of this mineral manifests itself in the appearance, at first, of a yellowish color on the edges of the older leaves, which extends to the veins, turning brown; if the deficiency is not corrected, the symptoms extend to the upper part of the plant, reducing vigor and photosynthetic activity.

CALCIUM: The symptoms of the deficiency of this element, are more clearly seen in the young leaves, in which there are clear white transparent spots near the edges and between the veins. The plants slow down their growth, the internodes shorten, especially at the apex, and the chlorosis between the veins increases gradually as the deficiency worsens.

<!-- image -->

AZOT: When deficiencies of this element, the growth decreases, remaining the leaves small, hanging and pale green or yellow; the edges of the new leaves turn markedly aserados. The correction of its deficit is made through the use of fertilizers that contain sulfur.

COBRE: The lack causes the plant's growth to be slower, shortening the internodes; the young leaves remain small and may appear chlorotic spots in the older ones. The leaves turn a bright green, the edges dry and curl a little

<!-- image -->

IRON: Its deficiency makes the young leaves exhibit a pale yellow color between the veins, at the same time that the fruits pale when the lack is severe, the leaves turn chlorotic from the tip to the base. This deficiency can appear in calcareous or high pH soils due to the blockage of iron.

MANGANESE: Its deficiency causes the development of mottled interveinal leaf spots in younger leaves; these then turn yellowish-white from the edges towards the center. When the deficiency is severe, the older leaves are most affected, eventually leading to their drying.

BORON: Symptoms of deficiency can appear when the first harvest is made. Growth is not affected, but there is stalk splitting, the older and middle leaves turn chlorotic and develop watery spots; young leaves deform without fully expanding; sometimes young and developed fruits also deform, with stripes similar to those caused by cold.

## POLLINATION:

With the active presence of pollinating insects, it has been proven that good commercial yields of fruits are possible. Among the insects, bees are the best pollinators, as they are specialized in this task and are normally readily available, easy to handle, and can be placed where desired when the first flowers appear. It is recommended to use a minimum of 3 well-populated hives for apple trees during flowering; special care should be taken to apply insecticides early in the morning or in the last hours of the afternoon, in order not to affect the beneficial insects.

## INTEGRATED PEST MANAGEMENT

To sustainably manage pests, it is not simply possible to stop using pesticides; however, carrying out an active program of preventive practices is the most recommended; such as:

## SEED QUALITY:

It is recommended to sow resistant or tolerant varieties or hybrids, to reduce the use of pesticides.

## PLANTING DATE:

Choosing the planting date allows the crop's susceptible periods to be staggered with high pest populations, significantly reducing damage.

## PLANTING DENSITY:

The planting density of the crop significantly influences competition between the crop and weeds; having a fairly dense foliage can modify the soil microclimate, so it is necessary to use the recommended spacings for cucumber crops, which are: 1.2 m between rows and 0.4 m between plants or seedlings for the summer; 1.5 m between rows and 0.4 m between plants or seedlings for the rainy season. This way, some diseases caused by fungi and bacteria can be prevented.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## MULCHING:

Mulching not only controls weeds but also contributes to the prevention of diseases caused by fungi and bacteria, when the row is removed from the base of the plants.

## CROP ROTATION:

Continuous planting of the same crop tends to concentrate pests in the soil; it is advisable to program plantings of different crops that are not of the same family, to break or disrupt the life cycles of specific insects for a particular crop.

## INTERCROPPING:

Intercropping contributes to pest control and better use of soil nutrients. This practice consists of intercropping a main crop with some plants that act as repellents for pests, for example, deadnettle, mint, oregano, basil, and others.

## ASSOCIATED CULTIVATION:

This system allows specialized pests that feed on a single crop to not feed on the entire crop; the same applies to pathogens that can easily spread from plant to plant. Also, the diversity of food can increase the populations of predators that feed on the pests.

## PHYSICAL BARRIERS:

These are used to prevent pests from reaching the plants; in the field, a series of materials such as corn stalk or corn chaff, nettle, and others can be used.

## PHYSICAL TRAPS:

These are practically physical barriers but have glue for the pests that arrive and stick to them, preventing them from escaping; pheromones, light traps, and yellow colors are used.

## REMOVAL OF HOST PLANTS:

This is a key practice in managing insect-transmitted diseases, especially those plants that are host plants for insects that transmit viruses.

## REMOVAL OF OLD CROP RESIDUES:

This is key for managing specific pests that cannot survive on other plants; when they are not fed, their populations quickly decline; therefore, it is necessary to destroy or incorporate the crop residues.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

## CURATIVE MEASURES:

Unfortunately, the use of preventive practices will not guarantee that there will be no economic damage from pests. Therefore, even if preventive methods are used, they must be supplemented with the following stages:

## SAMPLING AND CRITICAL LEVELS:

The basis for the rational use of pesticides is constant sampling of the crop. The only way to know if it is worth applying a pesticide is to go to the field and determine how abundant the pest is.

After analyzing the results of each sampling, you must decide whether you can coexist with the pests, or whether it is necessary to apply a pesticide, i.e., the loss caused by the pest must have at least the same cost of purchase and application of pesticide.

## APPLICATION METHOD:

## INSECTS:

## SAMPLING:

Before making a chemical application, it is important to perform a sampling, to determine the quantity and species of insects present, both beneficial and harmful. This sampling is done randomly, trying to cover an area representative of the cultivated plot, no less than 10 sampling points per hectare, each point must cover one square meter. Based on the results obtained, the decision is made as to which pests to combat and which products to apply.

Some of the main insects that attack cucumbers are:

Cutting Caterpillars: cutworms, rootworms, sawflies, cutters (Feltia subterranea, Agrotis sp, Prodenia sp).

## DAMAGE:

It is a group of insects known as "cutworms", "slugs", "cutters" and others, which are larvae that come from nocturnal butterflies with similar habits; during the day they remain hidden in the soil, near the base of the plants, being more active at night; at dusk they come out and go in search of the young stems; feeding on the roots and stems; they generally cut the stems of newly born plants at ground level.

<!-- image -->

In addition to the type of pesticide, the application method can determine the effectiveness of an application and its impact on natural enemies. You must consider the total volume of mixture to apply per apple, to what part of the plant the application will be directed, if you will use adjuvants or other non-toxic products to improve the application, and the time when you will apply.

## PESTS

## CONTROL:

Apply preventively, Carbofuran at a dose of 1.75 to 2.0 kgha, this product prevents the attack of nematodes. When massive attacks occur in newly emerged plantations, it is possible to use poisoned bait based on methyl or carbosil, preferably making applications after 5 p.m.

## Blind Chicken (Phyllophaga sp.)

## DAMAGE:

The adults are brown beetles, the female lays eggs in the soil at a depth of 2 to 10 cm in small groups under the cover of weeds and in the soil furrows, the eggs are white and shiny, round. With the first rains, the larvae begin to activate, moving towards the deeper layers of the soil, particularly in the area where the roots of the plants develop, they feed on them and on the bases of the stems, causing the death of the plants.

Squash Bugs (Diabrotica sp).

## DAMAGE:

Adults have an oval shape, some have green and yellow bands on the body, others have black or reddish-brown spots and yellow coloration; some are single-colored, and others have metallic coloration; they measure approximately 4 to 8 mm, their head is black and has long antennae; they attack the crop throughout its entire development cycle, starting with the greenest parts of the plants, they can completely defoliate young or small plants. The female lays eggs in the soil around the plants; its importance lies in the early stages of the crop.

Photo 21 Adult tortoise beetle (Diabrotica balteata)

<!-- image -->

## CONTROL:

Apply any of the following products: Teflubenzuron, 15 cc/4-gallon pump. Thiacloprid-cyflutrin, 25 cc/4-gallon pump. Lufenurom, 25 cc/4-gallon pump.

## Leaf Miner (Liriomyza sp).

## DAMAGE:

It is a small, yellowish-white larva, without legs, that mines leaves, building galleries. The adult larva transforms into a small fly, which lays eggs in the internal tissues of the leaves, where new larvae are born, which immediately begin to feed, making the semi-transparent galleries visible. Severe attacks can cause reductions in the harvest.

Aphids (Aphis gossypii).

## DAMAGE:

They are globular in shape, yellowish-green in color, and live in colonies on the underside of the leaves; the females are larger than the males and are very prolific, each one can originate a new colony without the need for males. Plants attacked by these aphids have folded edges on the terminal shoots and a wrinkled appearance; in severe attacks, the older leaves also have this appearance; the foliage becomes stunted and takes on a cinnamon color, causing the death of the plant.

## CONTROL:

Apply any of the following products:

Methyl oxydimeton,

50 gal 4-gallon pump.

Tioxiclan Hoxalato,

50 gal 4-gallon pump.

Tiametoxan,

14 gal 4-gallon pump.

## Pythium sp. and (Fusarium solani fs.) Disease

## DAMAGE:

Dark lesions are observed at the base of the stem, causing the plant to droop or rot, from the roots and stems, up to causing the death of newly emerged plants.

Apply any of the following products in a preventative manner:

Methyl thiophanate,

100 cc/4 gallon pump.

Carbendazim,

40 cc/4 gallon pump.

Propane carb,

50 cc/4 gallon pump.

Prochloraz,

40 cc/4 gallon pump.

Powdery Mildew (Erysiphe cichoracearum).

## DAMAGE:

It manifests on leaves and stems, with the appearance of white spots, which, when developed, turn powdery, resembling ash, and can cover the entire foliage. The leaves fall before the crop reaches maturity. The crop can be completely lost if the disease is allowed to develop freely.

This disease does not require high environmental humidity to spread, therefore it can also occur during the dry season (summer).

Photo 28. Symptom caused by Powdery Mildew

## CONTROL:

Apply any of the following products in a preventative manner:

Tebuconazole-triadimefon

25 cc/4 gallon pump.

Azoxystrobin,

14 g/4 gallon pump.

Prochloraz,

20 cchomba de 4 galones.

Propineb más Provalicab,

60 ghomba 4 galones.

Mildiu lanoso (Pseudoperonospora cubensis).

## DAMAGE:

## CONTROL:

It manifests during the rainy season when high temperatures and high humidity. The disease starts on the oldest leaves of the plant in the form of angular yellow spots, delimited by the veins of the leaves. Over time, they dry out, and the damage extends to the younger ones. If the conditions of humidity continue to be favorable, it can destroy the entire crop. The plants are not attacked, but they suffer from defoliation, becoming small, poorly formed, and scorched by the sun, and there is also a considerable reduction in production. When the days are well humid, in the early morning hours, cottony-looking fungal structures can be observed on the underside of the leaves. There is a lack of fruit.

## FRUIT ROT:

## DAMAGE:

This occurs when the fruits come into contact with the soil, causing watery rot, with the presence of the white cottony mycelium of the fungus on the fruit being observed. fruits

## CONTROL:

Prevent contact with the soil, so it is advisable to place a cover or "mulch", use stakes to hang the fruits, remove the damaged ones, and avoid waterlogging in the soil. fruits fruits '

## Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) and (ZMV)

## DAMAGE:

The crop presents mottled and deformed leaves; the fruits can also present mottled and deformed, slowing the growth of the plant. The viruses host certain weeds and are transmitted to the crop by aphids.

Photo 30, Symptoms caused by the Cucumber Mosaic Virus (ZYMV)

<!-- image -->

## CONTROL:

Weeds must be controlled within and around the planting; aphids must be controlled from the moment the first insects are observed in the field, and the plants with symptoms of virosis must be removed and taken out of the planting.

Nematodes, the nodular (Meloidogyne incógnita).

## DAMAGE:

## CONTROL:

Damages the roots of plants, causing wilting, yellowing, weakening, reduced growth, and failure to respond to fertilizer application. The most important damage caused by this nematode is the attack on the roots of plants, causing the formation of nodules or galls very noticeable in the affected areas, which is why it is called "nodular" or "galling".

Photo 32. Cucumber root damaged by Nematodes (Meloidogyne sp)

<!-- image -->

This nematode can be controlled by crop rotation, which includes the sowing of some grasses, good soil preparation, selection of tolerant varieties, and sowing in soils with good drainage. It is recommended to perform laboratory analyses periodically to determine the appropriate measures for its control; if nematodes are found, it is recommended to apply Carbofuran or Terbufos.

Photo 31, Symptoms caused by the Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV)

## WEEDS

Weeds compete with the crop for nutrients, water, and light, so frequent cleaning is required to prevent weeds in the first 45 days of crop establishment. They are also hosts for harmful insects and diseases. In El Salvador, the main weeds that affect cucurbitaceae are:

- Coyolillo (Cyperus rotundus) .

## Perennial Weeds.

- Barnacle (Cynodon dactylon).

## Annual Weeds.

- John's Sorghum (Sorghum halapense)
- Water Creeper (Echinochloa sp).
- Lettuce (Portulaca oleracea)
- Gallina (Euleusine indica)
- Amaranthus sp

Weed control can be carried out manually, mechanically and chemically; it gives better results to combine manual control with chemical.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Manual control is carried out using a hoe or a spade, it is preferable to use the spade, as with this tool the weed is pulled and turned over, achieving good control. The use of the hoe is better to use it near the plant.

Mechanical control occurs with the soil preparation and during the development of the planting. Once the crop is established, the control is carried out with a cultivator, normally this control must be accompanied by a manual action.

Chemical control, normally requires to be complemented with a manual labor, since the products do not cover the entire development period of the cucumber crop. It is recommended to apply herbicides only in the soil preparation, if selective post-emergence herbicides are applied in the early stages of the crop, it is necessary to take the necessary precautions to not damage the plants, in addition to remembering that the same herbicide application equipment (backpack sprayer) cannot be used to apply insecticides, fungicides and foliar fertilizers.

## HARVEST

The harvest dates vary from one cultivar to another and from environmental conditions. Varieties and hybrids for fresh consumption must be harvested between 50 and 65 days after planting and every 3 days to maintain the size of the fruit for quality purposes, harvesting the fruits in an immature state. For pickles, they must be harvested between 40 and 50 days after planting. The size of the fruit can vary from 20 to 30 cm in length and from 3 to 6 cm in diameter; in dark green or green color, without any signs of yellowing, when the angles or edges of the fruit tend to disappear or when the fruit becomes cylindrical, also when the thorns easily detach from the fruit.

Preferably, the harvest (cutting) of cucumbers should be carried out during the most fresh hours of the morning or in the last hours of the afternoon. The average number of cuts are 7-8, at 46, 49, 52, 55, 58, 63, 69 and 76 days after planting. During the harvest, the fruits are carefully separated from the plant in order to prolong the life of the fruit. It is best to cut the fruits with pruning shears and not to pull them; cucumbers for the market must be harvested by hand; careful handling is required to prevent mechanical damage, which can cause water loss and the development of diseases during storage. All fruits must be placed in plastic boxes or in wooden crates and transport them to the packing area as soon as possible. The boxes full in the field must be protected from direct exposure to sunlight, wind and rain.

## HARVEST INDEX:

- Physiological maturity (dark green and very firm fruit).
- Appropriate shape.
- Appropriate size according to variety or hybrid (especially diameter and length).
- Free of diseases
- Free of insect infestations, bruises, sunburn and other damage.

## POST HARVEST HANDLING

Cucumber is a product that can be stored satisfactorily for relatively short periods (15 to 20 days), as it easily loses quality. The most favorable storage temperature is 10 to 12°C, it can be stored at 8°C

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

but for a short time without causing damage by the cold. Fruits stored for 2 weeks at 5°C or less suffer from cold damage, the manifestations of cold damage are translucent and watery areas, accelerated attack and rot, this type of damage is cumulative and can start in the field before harvest. At 15°C, the fruits tend to ripen prematurely, becoming yellowish.

## COMMERCIALIZATION

Cucumbers, after being harvested, are selected according to quality standards: The fruit is packed in the field, in the plant or at the center of a wide variety of packaging systems that are used: baskets, wooden or cardboard crates and others. The most important thing in packaging and in selecting the type of packaging is the arrangement. The fruit must be placed in such a way as to minimize its movement within the packaging.

## QUALITY REQUIREMENTS

Cucumbers are classified by their maturity stage, and by size. Cucumbers are preferred for their cylindrical shape with a smooth and straight surface, dark green and uniform color (absence of yellowing), they are commercially sold clean, they must be firm when cut, and the inner ring should have a greater proportion of pulp and the seeds should be no more than 3 mm in size, with good moisture inside. When the cucumber breaks manually, it should emit a slight resistance sound, long, long,
